title: "Nutrient response in high-yielding Nebraska corn"

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      comment = "")
options(knitr.table.format = "pipe", knitr.kable.NA = "")
```

```{r load}
source(file.path("R", "99_utils.R"))
m <- read_metrics()
n <- function(k, digits = 2) formatC(metric_num(m, k), format = "f",
                                     digits = digits)
pct <- function(k, digits = 0) formatC(100 * metric_num(m, k), format = "f",
                                       digits = digits)
sci <- function(k, digits = 2) formatC(metric_num(m, k), format = "e",
                                       digits = digits)
tbl <- function(name) utils::read.csv(file.path("results",
                                                paste0(name, ".csv")),
                                      check.names = FALSE)
kab <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(x, row.names = FALSE, ...)
# p-values here span 165 orders of magnitude, so they are rendered in
# scientific notation rather than rounded to a column of zeros.
fmt_p <- function(p) formatC(p, format = "e", digits = 2)
```

This report presents the results written by `analysis/run_all.R`. It reads the
recorded quantities in `results/` rather than recomputing them, so that the
numbers here and the numbers a gate checks are the same numbers. The analysis
code lives in `R/`; this file calls into it and interprets what it produced.
The seed is `r format(metric_num(m, "seed"), scientific = FALSE)`.

## The experiment

The deposit holds `r n("data_rows", 0)` plot observations from
`r n("site_years", 0)` site-years of corn trials run in Nebraska between 2002
and 2004. Nine standard treatments were applied at every site-year, giving
`r n("standard_rows", 0)` plots in `r n("design_cells", 0)` design cells with
`r n("design_min_reps", 0)` to `r n("design_max_reps", 0)` replicate plots each
and no cell empty. The remaining `r n("excluded_rows", 0)` plots belong to
site-specific sub-trials present at between one and seven site-years, and are
excluded from every comparison below. Every site-year was irrigated, at rates
between `r n("irrigation_min_mm", 0)` and `r n("irrigation_max_mm", 0)` mm.

The nine treatments vary nitrogen across five rates and, at a fixed nitrogen
rate, omit phosphorus or potassium. That structure is what makes the phosphorus
and potassium questions answerable: the omission plots differ from the complete
treatment in one nutrient and nothing else.

```{r treatments}
ts <- tbl("treatment-summary")
names(ts) <- c("treatment", "plots", "site-years", "N", "P", "K", "S",
               "mean yield", "sd", "se")
kab(ts, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3),
    caption = "Applied rates in kg/ha and grain yield in Mg/ha.")
```

![Grain yield by treatment](../figures/fig01_yield_by_treatment.png)

## Where the variation lies

Mean grain yield over the standard plots is `r n("mean_yield")` Mg/ha with a
standard deviation of `r n("sd_yield")` Mg/ha, ranging from `r n("min_yield")`
to `r n("max_yield")` Mg/ha. Differences between site-years account for
`r pct("between_block_share_yield")` percent of the plot-level sum of squares.
A Nebraska field in a given season is therefore the largest single influence on
what a plot yields, which is why every comparison below is made within
site-years rather than across them.

![Distribution of plot yield](../figures/fig02_yield_distribution.png)

![The 34 site-years](../figures/fig05_site_years.png)

## Correlation structure, and where it misleads

The plant measurements are strongly redundant. Nutrient uptake is a tissue
concentration multiplied by a dry-matter mass that includes grain, and the
harvest indices are ratios among those same masses.

![Correlation among plant measurements](../figures/fig03_plant_correlations.png)

Pooled across all plots, grain yield and nitrogen uptake correlate at
`r n("pooled_r_yield_n_uptake")`. That coefficient survives disaggregation: the
weakest within-texture coefficient is
`r n("min_within_texture_r_yield_n_uptake")`, and within site-years the median
is `r n("median_within_block_r_yield_n_uptake")` with a minimum of
`r n("min_within_block_r_yield_n_uptake")`. No sign reverses, so the pooled
figure is not an aggregation artefact.

![Yield against nitrogen uptake by texture](../figures/fig04_yield_vs_n_uptake_by_texture.png)

Plant population behaves differently. Pooled, yield and population correlate at
`r n("pooled_r_yield_population")`; within site-years the coefficient falls as
low as `r n("min_within_block_r_yield_population")` and reverses sign in
`r n("population_sign_reversals_within_block", 0)` of the
`r n("standard_site_years", 0)` site-years. The pooled association largely
records that the fields planted at higher densities were the fields that yielded
more for other reasons, not that raising density within a field raised yield.
This is the one place in the data where a pooled correlation would have been
read wrongly.

```{r simpson}
sc <- tbl("subgroup-correlations")
sc <- sc[sc$grouping == "block", c("x", "y", "pooled_r", "n_groups",
                                   "min_within_r", "median_within_r",
                                   "max_within_r", "n_sign_reversals")]
names(sc) <- c("x", "y", "pooled r", "site-years", "min within",
               "median within", "max within", "sign reversals")
kab(sc, digits = 3,
    caption = "Pooled against within-site-year correlations with grain yield.")
```

## Dimension reduction

Principal components were fitted on the `r n("pca_n_vars", 0)` standardised
plant measurements, using the `r n("split_train_site_years", 0)` training
site-years only. Kaiser's criterion retains `r n("pca_n_retained", 0)`
components, accounting for `r pct("pca_variance_retained")` percent of total
variance; the first accounts for `r pct("pca_pc1_proportion")` percent and the
second for `r pct("pca_pc2_proportion")` percent.

![Component eigenvalues](../figures/fig07_pca_scree.png)

```{r loadings}
kab(tbl("pca-loadings"), digits = 3,
    caption = "Loadings on the retained components.")
```

![Plots in the first two components](../figures/fig08_pca_scores.png)

The components describe the redundancy among harvest measurements. They are not
used to predict yield, because grain yield is an algebraic component of several
of the variables they are built from.

## Clustering

The number of clusters was chosen by majority rule across the indices NbClust
computes, not fixed in advance: `r n("kmeans_index_votes", 0)` of
`r n("kmeans_indices_reporting", 0)` indices selected
k = `r n("kmeans_k", 0)`. The resulting partition accounts for
`r pct("kmeans_between_share")` percent of the total sum of squares.

```{r clusters}
kab(tbl("cluster-correspondence"), digits = 3,
    caption = "Association between cluster membership and candidate explanations.")
```

Cluster membership tracks site-year (Cramer's V
`r n("cramers_v_cluster_site_yr")`) far more closely than treatment
(`r n("cramers_v_cluster_treatment")`). The clusters recover which field a plot
was in, not what was applied to it.

![Clusters against field position](../figures/fig09_clusters.png)

## Treatment effects

The design is a randomised complete block with site-year as the block.

```{r anova}
av <- tbl("anova-rcb")
av$p <- ifelse(is.na(av$p), "", fmt_p(av$p))
av$f <- ifelse(is.na(av$f), "", formatC(av$f, format = "f", digits = 1))
kab(av, digits = c(0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 0),
    caption = "Analysis of variance on grain yield, blocked on site-year.")
```

Treatment affects yield (F = `r n("anova_treatment_f", 1)`,
p = `r sci("anova_treatment_p")`), as does site-year
(F = `r n("anova_block_f", 1)`). A multivariate test on grain yield, total dry
matter, ear number and nitrogen uptake jointly agrees (Pillai's trace
`r n("manova_treatment_pillai", 3)`, p = `r sci("manova_treatment_p")`).

The five pre-specified contrasts are estimated as paired differences of
site-year means across all `r n("standard_site_years", 0)` blocks, so that the
unit of inference is the site-year and not the plot.

```{r contrasts}
ct <- tbl("treatment-contrasts")
out <- data.frame(contrast = ct$contrast,
                  estimate = round(ct$estimate, 3),
                  `ci low` = round(ct$ci_low, 3),
                  `ci high` = round(ct$ci_high, 3),
                  p = fmt_p(ct$p), `p holm` = fmt_p(ct$p_holm),
                  check.names = FALSE)
kab(out,
    caption = "Paired contrasts on grain yield, Mg/ha, with 95 percent intervals.")
```

![Treatment contrasts](../figures/fig10_treatment_contrasts.png)

Applying nitrogen at the mid rate raised yield by
`r n("contrast_n0p1k1_to_n2p1k1_estimate")` Mg/ha
(95 percent interval `r n("contrast_n0p1k1_to_n2p1k1_ci_low")` to
`r n("contrast_n0p1k1_to_n2p1k1_ci_high")`). Raising nitrogen further to the
high rate added `r n("contrast_n2p1k1_to_n4p1k1_estimate")` Mg/ha
(`r n("contrast_n2p1k1_to_n4p1k1_ci_low")` to
`r n("contrast_n2p1k1_to_n4p1k1_ci_high")`).

Omitting phosphorus at a fixed nitrogen rate cost
`r n("contrast_n2p0k1_to_n2p1k1_estimate")` Mg/ha, with an interval from
`r n("contrast_n2p0k1_to_n2p1k1_ci_low")` to
`r n("contrast_n2p0k1_to_n2p1k1_ci_high")` that includes zero. Omitting
potassium changed yield by
`r n("contrast_n2p1k0_to_n2p1k1_estimate")` Mg/ha, and doubling both phosphorus
and potassium at the high nitrogen rate changed it by
`r n("contrast_n4p1k1_to_n4p2k2_estimate")` Mg/ha
(`r n("contrast_n4p1k1_to_n4p2k2_ci_low")` to
`r n("contrast_n4p1k1_to_n4p2k2_ci_high")`). At these soil test levels and
yields, none of the three intervals admits a phosphorus or potassium response
larger than about half a megagram per hectare.

### Assumptions

```{r assumptions}
kab(tbl("anova-assumptions"), digits = 4,
    caption = "Assumption tests for the plot-level analysis of variance.")
```

Both assumptions of the plot-level analysis of variance are violated. Residuals
depart from normality (W = `r n("shapiro_statistic", 4)`,
p = `r sci("shapiro_p")`) and variances differ across treatments
(p = `r sci("brown_forsythe_treatment_p")`), which is expected when one
treatment withholds nitrogen and yields both lower and more variably than the
rest. The F test is reported because it is robust at this sample size, but it is
not what the conclusions rest on.

```{r contrast-normality}
kab(tbl("contrast-normality"), digits = 4,
    caption = "Normality of the block differences the paired contrasts use.")
```

The paired contrasts require only that the
`r n("standard_site_years", 0)` block differences are approximately normal, and
they are: the smallest p across the five contrasts is
`r n("contrast_differences_min_shapiro_p", 3)`.

## Predicting yield on an unfamiliar field

A predictor was admitted only if its value is set or measurable before harvest.
That leaves `r n("n_allowed_predictors", 0)` predictors and excludes
`r n("n_blocked_predictors", 0)` harvest measurements. The exclusion is
arithmetic rather than cautious: total dry matter is the sum of grain, cob and
stover dry matter, an identity this data set satisfies to a maximum relative
error of `r sci("identity_max_error_dm")`, and harvest index is grain dry matter
divided by that sum.

Partitions are formed over site-years. A model is trained on
`r n("split_train_site_years", 0)` site-years and tested on the
`r n("split_test_rows", 0)` plots of the `r n("split_test_site_years", 0)` it
has never seen.

```{r models}
mm <- tbl("model-metrics")
kab(mm[, c("model", "role", "n_predictors", "n_test", "rmse", "mae", "r2")],
    digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3),
    caption = "Accuracy on held-out site-years. RMSE and MAE in Mg/ha.")
```

Because a single ten-site-year test set is a noisy basis for that claim, the
comparison is repeated leaving out one site-year at a time, so that every
site-year serves as an unfamiliar field exactly once.

```{r cv}
kab(tbl("cross-validation"), digits = c(0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3),
    caption = "Leave-one-site-year-out cross-validation over all 34 site-years.")
```

The random forest reaches RMSE `r n("cv_rf_rmse", 3)` Mg/ha and an R-squared of
`r n("cv_rf_r2", 3)`, against `r n("cv_mean_rmse", 3)` Mg/ha for predicting the
training mean. Roughly a fifth of plot-level yield variation is recoverable from
applied rates, plant stand, irrigation and a pre-season soil test. The rest
belongs to the field and the season.

![Predicted against observed](../figures/fig11_observed_vs_predicted.png)

![Variable importance](../figures/fig12_variable_importance.png)

### Two ways this number could have been inflated

Admitting harvest measurements as predictors raises the held-out R-squared from
`r n("rf_test_r2", 3)` to `r n("leakage_test_r2", 3)`. Almost all of that is the
identity above, reported back as accuracy.

Splitting over plots rather than site-years raises the held-out R-squared of the
same random forest from `r n("rf_test_r2", 3)` to
`r n("plot_split_rf_test_r2", 3)`. Replicate plots from one field in one season
are near-duplicates, and a plot-level split leaves copies of the test plots in
the training set. Both figures are reported in the table above as illustrations,
not as results.
